material: Not published by the manufacturer — Levoit's spec sheet lists no housing or tank material
features: Top-fill 6L tank — you never invert a full tank over the base
Built-in humidity sensor drives a genuine Auto mode to a 40-50% target
VeSync scheduling plus Alexa and Google voice control
Essential-oil tray injects aroma into the mist stream
Display-off sleep mode; Levoit rates the unit at 30dB or below

specs.technology: Ultrasonic cool mist — a piezoelectric disc shatters water into a visible aerosol that is blown out of a nozzle
specs.whiteDust: Yes, and there is no fix sold for it. the EPA's "Use and Care of Home Humidifiers" states that ultrasonic and impeller humidifiers "are very efficient at dispersing minerals in tap water into the air" and that they "can disperse materials, such as microorganisms and minerals, from their water tanks into indoor air". Levoit sells no demineralisation cartridge for the Classic 300S — the part in the box is an aroma pad and a water-filter sponge, neither of which removes dissolved minerals. TechGearLab's tester warns that on tap water the minerals "eventually start to be noticeable on your furniture". Distilled water is the only real remedy, at roughly $1-1.50 per gallon
specs.outputPerDay: Not published by the manufacturer — Levoit publishes runtime and a 26W rated power but no mL/hr or gallons-per-day output figure anywhere on the spec sheet
specs.runtimeQuoted: "Up to 60 hours" — Levoit's own page attaches that figure to the LOW mist setting. 6 L over 60 h is only about 100 mL/hr; on high the same tank empties in a small fraction of that time
specs.humidistat: Real closed-loop humidistat. An onboard humidity sensor feeds Auto mode, which holds 40-50% RH or a custom setpoint; TechGearLab called the auto mode "decently accurate"
specs.noiseLevel: Levoit claims 30dB or less. TechGearLab measured 38.5dB and describes an ultrasonic whine plus a steady dripping noise as the tank empties — a bedroom-relevant gap between claim and measurement
specs.consumables: No wick and no demineralisation cartridge exist for this model, so the strictly required consumable cost is $0/yr. In practice the running cost is distilled water — roughly $1-1.50 a gallon, or about $45-90 over a 60-day heating season at one tank every two days
specs.cleaningBurden: Above average. The top-fill opening takes an adult hand and the vapour tower has clearance around it; TechGearLab scored cleaning 8.5/10 but flagged small crevices in the base. Nothing is dishwasher-safe. The EPA advice is to "clean portable humidifiers every third day"
specs.antimicrobial: None claimed. No UV lamp, no silver-ion or antimicrobial coating, no bacteriostatic additive supported
specs.mistTemperature: Cool mist at room temperature — no burn risk, but equally no thermal kill step, so whatever is living in the tank is aerosolised with the water

pros: One of the few sub-$100 humidifiers with a genuine closed-loop humidistat rather than a timer wearing a humidity label
6L top-fill tank goes two nights between refills at bedroom output levels
Auto mode plus app scheduling actually works unattended — TechGearLab rated the humidity tracking accurate
Cleaning access is unusually good for an ultrasonic: wide top opening, clearance round the tower
cons: Ultrasonic, so it aerosolises every mineral in the water as white dust on furniture and into the air, and Levoit sells no demineralisation cartridge for it — distilled water is the only fix
Levoit publishes no output figure at all: no mL/hr, no gallons per day, so the "215-505 ft²" coverage claim cannot be checked against anything
The "up to 60 hours" runtime is the low setting only; run it on high in a genuinely dry room and you are refilling daily
Measured 38.5dB against a claimed 30dB, with an audible ultrasonic whine and dripping as the tank drains
No antimicrobial or UV stage of any kind, so the every-third-day cleaning the EPA recommends is the entire hygiene plan
shortTagline: The smart ultrasonic everyone buys — and the one that will powder your nightstand.

features: Evaporative, so it emits invisible vapour and never produces white dust
6-gallon reservoir with a fill hose you run straight from a tap
Dry Mode runs the fan alone to dry the four wicks and slow mould growth
Collapsible body with wheels and a storage bag for the off-season
36W DC motor — a fraction of the draw of an AC-motor console

specs.technology: Evaporative — a fan pulls room air through four wick filters standing in the reservoir; moisture leaves as invisible vapour, minerals stay in the wick
specs.whiteDust: None. Evaporative humidifiers leave dissolved minerals behind in the wick — that is exactly why the wick goes stiff and crusty. Tap water is fine and no distilled water is needed
specs.tankCapacity: 6 gal / 22.7 L reservoir, filled through a supplied hose and funnel
specs.outputPerDay: Not published by Levoit as a gallons-per-day figure. The only published throughput is 6 gallons over "up to 72 hours", which works out at roughly 2 gal/day at the setting that runtime is quoted for
specs.runtimeQuoted: "Up to 72 hours" — Levoit does not state the fan speed, but 6 gal / 72 h is about 2 gal/day, i.e. a low-to-mid setting. On high it is materially shorter
specs.coverage: Up to 3,000 ft² claimed with 360° circulation — the largest claim in this set, and one no portable unit can meet in a house with closed doors
specs.humidistat: Real closed-loop humidistat with a target-RH setpoint, plus app-side humidity history in VeSync
specs.noiseLevel: 28-48 dB across the speed range per Levoit's material. The low end is genuinely bedroom-quiet; the top end is a fan you will hear
specs.consumables: Four wick filters, replaced together. Levoit's 4-pack is $39.99 and is listed as lasting up to 6 months, so about $40-80/yr depending on water hardness and hours. Dry Mode exists specifically to stretch that interval
specs.cleaningBurden: Low by console standards but not trivial: the reservoir is wide open and the parts nest for storage, but four wet wicks sit in standing water and Dry Mode has to be run to keep them from souring. Nothing is dishwasher-safe
specs.antimicrobial: No UV lamp and no antimicrobial claim on the water path. Levoit's hygiene answer is Dry Mode plus wick replacement, not a kill stage
specs.mistTemperature: Cool, invisible vapour at room temperature — no burn risk. The evaporative process itself does not carry minerals or tank water into the air

pros: Evaporative design means no white dust and no distilled-water habit — you fill it from the tap with a hose
Six gallons and up to 72 hours is the longest unattended run here without stepping up to a plumbed whole-house unit
Dry Mode is a real answer to the wet-wick problem most evaporative units ignore
36W and 28dB at the low end make it far quieter and cheaper to run than an AC-motor console of similar output
Collapses with wheels and a storage bag, which matters for something this big six months of the year
cons: $249.99 plus roughly $40-80 a year in wicks — the highest first-year cost of any evaporative unit here except the Venta
The 3,000 ft² claim is a still-air marketing number; a single portable unit will not humidify a 3,000 ft² house with interior doors shut
Levoit publishes no gallons-per-day output at all, so you have to back it out of the 6 gal / 72 h runtime
Four wicks standing in six gallons of water is a lot of wet surface — skip Dry Mode and skip the wick changes and it will smell
Physically large even collapsed, and there is nowhere on the unit to see humidity without the phone
shortTagline: Six gallons of invisible, dust-free humidity for a whole floor, at a filter-fed price.

model: Honeywell HCM350 Germ Free Cool Mist Humidifier (HCM350W / HCM350B)
material: Plastic housing; Honeywell's manual states the water tank and water tray are top-rack dishwasher safe below 158°F on a light or normal cycle
connectivity: No wireless connectivity — three-position mechanical rotary control only
features: UV chamber treats the water before it reaches the wick
Protec HAC-504AW antimicrobial wicking filter traps minerals so nothing white leaves the unit
Water tank and tray are top-rack dishwasher safe — rare in this category
Rated 2 gallons of moisture output per day from a 1.1 gallon tank
Three-year Honeywell warranty, the longest of the mainstream evaporative units

specs.technology: Evaporative wick with a UV chamber in the water tray — a fan pulls air through the wet HAC-504AW filter
specs.whiteDust: None. The mineral load stays in the wick, which is why Honeywell's manual explains that brown or rust-coloured "mineral deposit" staining on the filter is normal and does not affect performance. Tap water is fine
specs.outputPerDay: "2 US gallons (7.6 liters) output per day" per Honeywell's own manual — which is nearly twice the tank. Meeting the rated output means filling the 1.1 gal tank roughly twice a day, not once
specs.runtimeQuoted: "Up to 24 hours" — on the LOW of three settings. That is 1.1 gal in 24 h, which is barely half the rated 2 gal/day output; the two headline numbers describe two different settings
specs.coverage: Sources conflict: Honeywell's own product page says only "medium room" with no square footage, while FiltersFast's listing for the same model states 500-800 ft²
specs.humidistat: None. Three fixed output speeds on a mechanical dial, no humidity sensor, no auto mode and no auto shut-off when the tank runs dry — you are the humidistat
specs.noiseLevel: Not published as a decibel figure by Honeywell; the product page says only "quiet operation". It is a 60W fan drawing air through a wet wick, so the top speed is clearly audible
specs.consumables: Two separate consumables. The HAC-504 "Filter A" wick is $32.95 for a Honeywell 3-pack (a compatible FiltersFast 3-pack is $22.99) and Honeywell says replace it every 30-60 days. On top of that the Protec antimicrobial cartridge is a 30-day item. A full heating season is realistically $40-70
specs.cleaningBurden: Among the best here. The tank and tray go on the dishwasher's top rack, the tank opening takes a hand, and the manual's disinfection routine is one teaspoon of bleach per gallon. Honeywell says only that it "requires regular cleaning" without naming an interval; the EPA says every third day
specs.antimicrobial: Two claims, both qualified. The UV chamber is rated "Up to 99.9% Germ Free*", where the asterisk in Honeywell's own manual ties it to independent testing of microbial reduction after two hours of UV exposure — a water-tray claim, not an air claim. The wick itself is separately treated as a Protec antimicrobial filter
specs.mistTemperature: Cool, invisible vapour at room temperature — no burn risk at all, which is why this is the standard nursery recommendation

pros: Evaporative plus UV: no white dust, no distilled water, and a genuine (if narrowly worded) kill stage on the water
Tank and tray are top-rack dishwasher safe, which almost nothing else in this category can say
2 gal/day rated output is real humidification, not a desktop trickle
Three-year warranty and a filter supply chain that has existed for fifteen years — parts are trivially available
cons: No humidistat, no auto mode and no auto shut-off — it runs until you stop it, and the FiltersFast listing states the omission outright
The 2 gal/day output and the 24-hour runtime cannot both be true at once: the 1.1 gal tank means hitting rated output requires two fills a day
Two stacked consumables — a $23-33 three-pack of wicks every 30-60 days plus a 30-day Protec cartridge
Honeywell publishes no square footage and no decibel rating; retailers fill the gap with a 500-800 ft² figure Honeywell does not make
Honeywell's own store now marks the HCM350 discontinued and points buyers at the HEV320W, even though the model is still stocked and supported elsewhere
shortTagline: A fifteen-year-old evaporative workhorse with UV — and no humidistat at all.

model: Honeywell HWM845B Filter Free Warm Mist Humidifier
material: Plastic housing with a metal heating element inside a sealed boiling chamber
connectivity: No wireless connectivity — illuminated power switch and a two-position knob
features: Water is boiled in a dedicated chamber, so the vapour leaves genuinely sterilised
Filter-free — no wick, no cartridge required for it to run
Essential-oil cup built into the lid
Wide tank opening that takes a hand for cleaning and refilling
Auto shut-off and a refill indicator light

specs.technology: Warm mist — Honeywell's manual: "The tank feeds water into the boiling chamber where it is heated to a steam vapor". A resistive element does the boiling; there is no fan and no wick
specs.whiteDust: None. Boiling leaves minerals behind as scale in the chamber rather than aerosolising them, which is the whole reason warm-mist and steam units are dust-free — and also why the chamber needs descaling
specs.outputPerDay: Not published by the manufacturer — neither Honeywell's manual nor its store page gives a gallons-per-day or mL/hr figure for the HWM845
specs.runtimeQuoted: "Up to 24 hours" — Honeywell's store page attaches this to the LOW of two comfort settings. On high, a 1-gallon tank boiled away goes very much faster
specs.coverage: Sources conflict: Walmart's listing for the HWM845B says 400 ft², office-supply listings for the identical SKU say 520 ft², and Honeywell's own store page says only "medium" room
specs.humidistat: None. Two fixed comfort settings on a knob, no humidity sensor, no auto mode. There is an auto shut-off for an empty tank, which is a safety cut-out and not humidity control
specs.noiseLevel: Not published as a decibel figure. There is no fan, so the only noise is the boil itself — genuinely among the quietest ways to humidify a bedroom, at the cost of the heat
specs.consumables: Nothing is required — it is filter-free. Honeywell offers the optional Protec PC2V1 antimicrobial cleaning cartridge on a 30-day cycle (roughly $20-30/yr if you use it), but the unit runs without it
specs.cleaningBurden: Honeywell's manual says "Weekly cleaning is recommended" and prescribes two cups of distilled white vinegar in the reservoir for 20 minutes to strip scale, plus a separate bleach disinfection. The tank opening is wide; nothing is dishwasher-safe. Skip the descaling and the element fouls and output collapses
specs.antimicrobial: Boiling is the kill stage — no UV lamp and no antimicrobial wick. The optional Protec cartridge is a tank-side cleaning aid, not a certified disinfection claim
specs.mistTemperature: Boiled. Honeywell's manual is explicit: "DO NOT touch the steam vapor. Steam can cause burns" and the unit "produces hot steam". The output is genuinely sterile; the trade-off is a reservoir of near-boiling water in the room

pros: The vapour is genuinely sterilised by boiling — no white dust and no aerosolised tank bacteria, unlike any ultrasonic here
No fan means no fan noise; for a light sleeper this is quieter than any wick or ultrasonic unit in this set
Truly filter-free — there is no consumable you are required to buy, which over three years undercuts the evaporative units badly
Three-year Honeywell warranty at $54.95, and a wide tank opening you can get a hand into
cons: It boils water in a child's bedroom; Honeywell's own manual warns the steam "can cause burns" and to keep it away from children
No humidistat whatsoever — two knob positions and nothing that senses the room
Weekly vinegar descaling is not optional: mineral scale on the heating element is what kills these units, and Honeywell's manual prescribes the routine
Retail listings disagree on coverage — 400 ft² at Walmart versus 520 ft² on office-supply listings for the same SKU — and Honeywell publishes no number at all
No published output figure, so the only throughput data point is a 1-gallon tank over 24 hours on low
shortTagline: Genuinely sterile boiled steam for $55, and a scalding chamber to go with it.

model: Vicks Warm Steam Vaporizer V150 (V150SGN / V150RY series)
material: Plastic housing; the steam unit carries a carbon element that sheds harmless black flakes as it wears
connectivity: No wireless connectivity — single on/off switch, no output control
features: Boils the water outright, so the steam leaves sterile and dust-free
1.5 gallon tank — the largest tank of any sub-$25 humidifier here
Two scent-pad slots for Vicks VapoPads and a medicine cup for VapoSteam
Steam Guard shield over the steam outlet
Auto shut-off when the tank empties, plus a night light

specs.technology: Warm steam vaporizer. Current is passed through the water itself to boil it, which is why Vicks' own FAQ states "These units require water with minerals in it in order to function properly" — pure water does not conduct, so the unit will simply not steam
specs.whiteDust: None. Boiling drops the minerals out as scale inside the steam unit rather than aerosolising them. The visible particulate this unit does emit is black, not white: Vicks' cleaning instructions tell you to flush it "until black particles are no longer emitted", and those are carbon from the element
specs.outputPerDay: Not published by the manufacturer as a gallons-per-day or mL/hr figure. The only throughput anchor is the tank divided by the quoted runtime
specs.runtimeQuoted: Sources conflict: Vicks' own product page says "up to 24 hours", Target's listing for the same V150SGN says 18 hours. There is no output setting to attribute either figure to — the unit has one speed
specs.coverage: Sources conflict: Vicks' page and Walmart's listing say 600 ft², Target's listing for the same model says 300-500 ft²
specs.humidistat: None, and no output control either. One switch. It boils at full rate until the tank is empty or you unplug it — the single most over-humidification-prone unit in this set
specs.noiseLevel: Not published. There is no fan, so the noise is the boil; users describe intermittent gurgling and, when scaled or over-salted, spitting
specs.consumables: None required — no filter, no wick, no cartridge. VapoPads and VapoSteam are optional add-ons Vicks would like to sell you; the unit runs on plain tap water
specs.cleaningBurden: Weekly, and the routine is specific: Vicks says soak the steam unit "in 4 inches of white vinegar for 10 minutes", flush until black particles stop, then disinfect the reservoir with "1 teaspoon of bleach per gallon" for 20 minutes. The tank opening is wide. Scale build-up is what causes the spitting complaints
specs.antimicrobial: Boiling is the entire hygiene mechanism, and Vicks makes no germ-free or sterilisation marketing claim for it anywhere in the FAQ
specs.mistTemperature: Boiling. Vicks' placement guidance is to keep the vaporizer "at least four feet away from bedside" on a heat-resistant, waterproof surface. A 638W element and 1.5 gallons of near-boiling water is a scald hazard a toddler can pull over

pros: Under $20 for 1.5 gallons of genuinely sterile, dust-free steam — nothing else here is close on price per gallon
Zero consumables: no wick, no cartridge, no distilled water, nothing to buy again
No fan, so there is no fan noise, and a three-year Vicks warranty at this price
Wide tank opening and a published, specific weekly vinegar-and-bleach cleaning routine
cons: It cannot run on distilled or heavily filtered water. Vicks' own FAQ tells you to add "one or two pinches (1/8 tsp) of salt" — up to half a teaspoon — and warns that "too much salt can cause excessive boiling or blow a fuse"
638W of boiling water with no output control and no humidistat: one switch, full rate, until the tank runs dry
Real scald risk — Vicks says keep it four feet from the bed on a heat-resistant surface, which makes it a poor choice for a toddler's room despite the branding
Vicks and its own retailers disagree on both runtime (24h vs 18h) and coverage (600 ft² vs 300-500 ft²) for the same SKU
Emits black carbon flakes as the element wears, and the weekly vinegar flush is mandatory rather than advisory
shortTagline: $20 of boiled steam that literally will not run on distilled water.

material: ABS and polypropylene; the tank, cap and tray are dishwasher-safe
connectivity: No wireless connectivity — backlit capacitive controls on the unit
features: Mist-free evaporative design — nothing visible leaves the unit, so no damp surfaces
Tank, cap and tray all go in the dishwasher
UV LED treats the water before it reaches the wick
Smart Persistent Airflow runs the fan to dry the internals when water is detected
Adjustable white noise and a red or warm-white reading light

specs.technology: Evaporative and deliberately mist-free — a fan draws air through a paper wick past a UV LED. No aerosol is produced at all
specs.whiteDust: None, by design. Minerals are captured in the paper filter rather than thrown into the air, which is the single strongest argument for the whole Canopy concept and the reason it can honestly advertise tap-water operation
specs.tankCapacity: 2.5 L / 0.66 gal — the smallest reservoir in this set
specs.outputPerDay: Not published by Canopy. AirQualityNest's review measured roughly 150 mL/hr, which is about 3.6 L (0.95 gal) a day if it ran flat out — more than the tank holds
specs.runtimeQuoted: "Up to 36 hours" — that requires the low setting. AirQualityNest reports refills every 16 to 36 hours depending on the setting, and that it took nine hours to lift a room to 45% RH against three and a half hours for an ultrasonic Levoit
specs.coverage: Up to 500 ft² claimed (Anthropologie and Canopy list the same figure); Target's listing for the 2.5L unit says 300-500 ft²
specs.humidistat: Not a closed loop. Canopy offers low, medium, high and an "auto" mode that Target's listing describes as light-sensitive — i.e. it responds to room light, not to humidity. No humidity readout on the unit
specs.noiseLevel: Not published as a decibel figure. It is a small fan, and Canopy sells the sound as a feature — there is a deliberate adjustable white-noise function layered on top
specs.consumables: The most expensive consumable habit here. Canopy's own filter is $17 one-off, $14 as a single purchase or $12 on a 45-day subscription, and Canopy says replace every 45 days (Target and the Amazon 3-pack both say every six weeks). That is roughly eight filters a year — about $96-136/yr, more than half the price of the machine
specs.cleaningBurden: The best in this set. The tank, cap and tray are genuinely dishwasher-safe, the filter is disposable so there is nothing to scrub, and Smart Persistent Airflow dries the internals between runs. This is the one unit where the every-few-days cleaning advice is realistic to actually follow
specs.antimicrobial: An embedded UV LED treats the water and Canopy's filter has an antimicrobial core. AirQualityNest reports the UV claim as 99.9% of bacteria in the water before evaporation — a water-side claim, not an air-purification claim
specs.mistTemperature: Cool, invisible vapour — no burn risk, no wet surfaces, and nothing to knock over that is hot

pros: Mist-free evaporative with a UV stage: no white dust, no wet nightstand, tap water fine
Tank, cap and tray are dishwasher-safe — the only unit here where following hygiene advice takes no effort
Smart Persistent Airflow dries the wet internals automatically, which is a real answer to the mould problem evaporative units have
Genuinely pleasant as a bedside object — adjustable white noise, red reading light, and no glowing plume
cons: The filters cost roughly $96-136 a year at Canopy's own 45-day interval — after 18 months you have spent more on paper than on the humidifier
2.5L is the smallest reservoir here, and the "36 hours" is the low setting; in practice it is a daily refill
Slow: AirQualityNest measured nine hours to bring a room to 45% RH versus three and a half for a comparable ultrasonic
No humidistat — the "auto" mode reacts to room light, not to humidity, so nothing closes the loop
$159 with a one-year warranty, against three years on humidifiers costing a third as much
shortTagline: No mist, no white dust, dishwasher-safe — and about $120 a year in paper filters.

material: Stainless steel tank, base and lid — the only all-metal water path in this comparison
connectivity: No wireless connectivity — three mist settings and a timer on the unit
features: Three stainless steel parts, all of which can be boiled to sterilise
No filter, no cartridge and no wick to buy, ever
4L tank with a completely open top — you can reach every internal surface
Three mist levels plus a built-in timer
Steel water path resists the biofilm that grows in plastic tanks

specs.technology: Ultrasonic cool mist in a stainless steel tank — a piezo disc still produces the aerosol; the metal changes the hygiene, not the physics
specs.whiteDust: Yes. Stainless steel solves the biofilm problem, not the mineral problem. the EPA's "Use and Care of Home Humidifiers" states that ultrasonic and impeller humidifiers "are very efficient at dispersing minerals in tap water into the air" and that they "can disperse materials, such as microorganisms and minerals, from their water tanks into indoor air", and Carepod sells no demineralisation cartridge — the design is explicitly filter-free. Distilled water remains the only way to avoid dust from a Carepod
specs.outputPerDay: Not published by the manufacturer as a mL/hr or gallons-per-day figure. Third-party spec sheets give 30 hours on low and roughly 10 hours on high from 4 L, implying about 133 mL/hr low and 400 mL/hr high
specs.runtimeQuoted: "Lasts 30 hrs" — that is the LOW setting. Third-party spec sheets put the high setting at roughly 10 hours from the same 4 L, a three-to-one spread
specs.coverage: Sources conflict badly: Carepod's own page says up to 500 ft², while a third-party spec sheet for the MS031S2 lists 92 ft² and flags it as probably a data error. Carepod publishes no output figure to arbitrate between them
specs.humidistat: Sources conflict. Carepod's own material describes three mist settings and a timer with no humidity readout on the unit; one third-party spec sheet lists a humidistat. There is no humidity display, so treat it as open-loop until Carepod publishes otherwise
specs.noiseLevel: Not published as a decibel figure — Carepod says only "whisper quiet". It is a 29W ultrasonic with no fan, so the noise floor is the ultrasonic hum plus water movement
specs.consumables: None. No filter, no wick, no cartridge, no antimicrobial additive — over five years this is the cheapest unit here to keep running, provided you are willing to buy distilled water
specs.cleaningBurden: The best-engineered cleaning story in this set. Three stainless parts, an entirely open top you can put a whole hand into, and Carepod's claim of "99.9% sterilizable against germs, bacteria, & mold" by boiling or hand washing. Note that the manufacturer describes the parts as hand-washable and boilable; retail listings that call them dishwasher-safe go beyond what Carepod's own page says
specs.antimicrobial: No UV and no coating — the claim is material-based. Steel does not harbour the biofilm plastic tanks do, and the parts can be boiled, which is a stronger real-world hygiene story than a UV lamp in a plastic tray
specs.mistTemperature: Cool mist only, at room temperature. No warm mode, no heater, no burn risk — and no thermal kill on the water leaving the unit

pros: Three stainless parts you can literally boil — the only unit here that solves the humidifier-hygiene problem rather than papering over it with a cartridge
Zero consumables for the life of the machine: no wick, no cartridge, no antimicrobial additive
Completely open tank top; there is no crevice you cannot reach with a hand and a cloth
Steel water path avoids the plastic-tank biofilm that makes cheap ultrasonics smell after a season
cons: It is still ultrasonic, so it still throws every dissolved mineral into the room as white dust — and being filter-free by design, there is no cartridge you can add
$279 with a one-year warranty, against $40 units carrying five years
No humidity readout and no confirmed humidistat; Carepod's own material describes settings and a timer, and third-party spec sheets contradict each other
The 30-hour runtime is the low setting — third-party sheets put the high setting near 10 hours from the same 4L tank
Carepod publishes no output figure and no decibel rating, and its coverage claim is contradicted by third-party data (500 ft² vs 92 ft²)
shortTagline: Three stainless parts you can boil — but it is ultrasonic, so distilled water only.

material: Plastic housing over a stack of rotating discs presenting 22.5 ft² of wetted surface
connectivity: No wireless connectivity — three-position mechanical fan-speed switch
features: Filter-free: a rotating disc stack does the evaporating, so there is no wick to replace
22.5 ft² of wetted disc surface — far more evaporative area than a wick unit
Draws 3 to 8 watts, an order of magnitude below every other unit here
Rated 24 dB(A) on its lowest speed
Cold-evaporation design that also traps some airborne dust in the water

specs.technology: Evaporative "airwasher" — a stack of rotating plastic discs carries a continuously renewed water film through the airstream. No wick and no aerosol
specs.whiteDust: None. Minerals stay in the water and end up as scale on the discs, which is why Venta specifies a 10-14 day cleaning cycle. Tap water is explicitly supported
specs.outputPerDay: Not published by the manufacturer — Venta publishes coverage, disc surface area, noise and wattage but no evaporation rate in litres or gallons per day for the LW25 Original
specs.runtimeQuoted: Not published as a runtime figure. Venta quotes capacity and coverage rather than hours, which without an output figure leaves the refill interval genuinely unknown from published data
specs.coverage: Up to 430 ft² at 8 ft ceilings (Venta, Lowe's and Walmart all agree). Venta's own LW25 Comfort Plus is rated 485 ft² from a smaller 1.8 gal tank
specs.humidistat: None on the Original — three fixed fan speeds and nothing that senses the room. Venta's own Comfort Plus version of the same LW25 is the model that adds a "digital hygrostat for measuring and controlling the relative humidity" plus auto and sleep modes, for $399.99. Evaporative physics self-limits as the room approaches saturation, but that is not a control loop
specs.noiseLevel: 24 / 34 / 44 dB(A) across the three speeds — the only unit here with a per-speed decibel figure published by the manufacturer, and the 24 dB low speed is the quietest genuinely measured figure in this set
specs.consumables: No filters ever — that is the pitch. But Venta prescribes its own chemistry: Water Treatment Additive at $17.99 used at each 10-14 day maintenance, and Venta Humidifier Cleaner at $16.99 roughly every six months. At Venta's own intervals that is a real recurring cost, not zero
specs.cleaningBurden: Every 10 to 14 days per Venta, which is more often than most owners expect from a "maintenance-free" machine. The upper housing lifts off the water basin and the disc stack pulls out; nothing is dishwasher-safe, and the disc stack is the fiddly part
specs.antimicrobial: No UV and no antimicrobial coating. The hygiene mechanism is the Water Treatment Additive plus the prescribed cleaning cycle — a consumable chemical, not a device feature
specs.mistTemperature: Cold evaporation at room temperature — no heat, no burn risk, no visible plume, and nothing carried out of the water

pros: Genuinely filter-free evaporation — no wick, no cartridge, no consumable that gates whether the machine works
3 to 8 watts. Over a heating season it costs a fraction of the AIRCARE console's 80W to run
24 dB(A) on low, published per speed by the manufacturer — the quietest verified figure in this comparison
No white dust and no distilled water; the disc stack means it also pulls some airborne dust into the water
Two-year warranty on a design that is mechanically simple enough to last a decade
cons: $299.99 for a machine with no humidistat at all — Venta sells the hygrostat as a separate $399.99 Comfort Plus model of the same LW25
"Filter-free" is not "consumable-free": Venta's own maintenance calls for $17.99 Water Treatment Additive at every 10-14 day service and $16.99 cleaner twice a year
Venta publishes no output rate and no runtime, so there is no way to compute the refill interval from the spec sheet
A 10-14 day cleaning cycle with a disc stack to pull and rinse is more hands-on than the marketing implies
430 ft² coverage for the price of two whole-house evaporative consoles
shortTagline: Filter-free evaporation that runs on 8 watts — with no humidistat at $300.

model: AIRCARE MA1201 Whole-House Console Evaporative Humidifier
connectivity: No wireless connectivity — digital control panel with a control lock
features: 12 gallons of moisture output per day — by far the highest here
Digital humidistat adjustable from 25% to 65% RH in 5% steps
Four fan speeds plus an auto mode that modulates speed to hold the setpoint
Casters, a refill indicator and a wick-change indicator
MAF1 SuperWick belt included in the box

specs.technology: Evaporative console — a four-speed fan pulls air through a large MAF1 SuperWick belt standing in the reservoir
specs.whiteDust: None. All the mineral load ends up in the wick, which is precisely why AIRCARE tells you the wick life depends on water hardness. Tap water is the intended input
specs.outputPerDay: 12 gallons per day — the highest rated output in this comparison, and more than three times what the tank holds. Hitting the rated figure means refilling 3.6 gallons roughly three times in 24 hours
specs.runtimeQuoted: "Up to 36 hours" — that is 3.6 gal over 36 h, i.e. 2.4 gal/day, which is one fifth of the 12 gal/day rated output. The two headline numbers describe opposite ends of the fan range
specs.coverage: Up to 3,600 ft² in tight construction, or about 2,500 ft² average per AIRCARE's own literature. Sylvane's listing for the same unit reproduces the figure with a typographical error (36,600 ft²)
specs.humidistat: Real closed-loop digital humidistat, adjustable 25-65% RH in 5% increments, with an auto mode that varies fan speed to hold the setpoint plus a dry-out mode and auto shut-off. The most capable humidity control in this set
specs.noiseLevel: Not published as a decibel figure by AIRCARE. It is an 80W fan moving enough air to evaporate twelve gallons a day — speed 4 is loud, and this is a living-room machine rather than a bedside one
specs.consumables: MAF1 SuperWick belts. AIRCARE's own guidance is one per season, but Home Depot's listing for the MAF1 states wicks "can last anywhere from 30 to 90 days, depending on the quality of your water", at $23.09 each. On hard water that is $70-90 a season, not one $23 wick
specs.cleaningBurden: Console-sized. The reservoir base is wide open and easy to wipe, the bottles unscrew for filling, and there is a dry-out mode — but nothing is dishwasher-safe and a 3.6 gallon standing reservoir is the largest body of stagnant water here if you let it sit
specs.antimicrobial: No UV and no built-in antimicrobial stage. AIRCARE sells a bacteriostatic treatment and demineralisation cartridges as separate accessories; neither ships in the box
specs.mistTemperature: Cool, invisible vapour at room temperature. No heat and no aerosol, but the sheer size and a 3.6 gallon water load make it a tipping hazard rather than a burn one

pros: 12 gal/day is genuine whole-floor humidification — nothing else here is within a factor of five
A real digital humidistat with 5% setpoint granularity, an auto fan mode and a dry-out cycle
Evaporative, so no white dust, no distilled water and no aerosolised tank water anywhere in the house
Casters, a wick-change indicator and a $23 commodity wick that every hardware store stocks
cons: The 12 gal/day output and the 3.6 gal tank are irreconcilable: run it at rated output and you are carrying water to it three times a day
80W of fan noise at speed 4 — this is not a bedroom unit, and AIRCARE publishes no decibel figure at all
Wick life is quoted by AIRCARE as one per season but by Home Depot as 30-90 days depending on water hardness; on hard water that is $70-90 a season in $23.09 wicks
Prices for the identical unit range from $149.99 at Sylvane to $187.99 on AIRCARE's own store — shop it, do not accept the first number
No antimicrobial or demineralisation stage in the box; both are accessories AIRCARE sells separately
shortTagline: Twelve gallons a day for a whole house, from a tank you refill three times a day.

features: 6L top-fill tank with both cool and pre-heated mist modes
Humidity sensor Dreo rates at ±5%, settable from 30% to 90% RH
500 mL/hr in warm mode, 300 mL/hr in cool mode — one of the few units that publishes output
Dual aroma-pad tray so you can switch scents without draining anything
App logs up to 30 days of room humidity history

specs.technology: Ultrasonic, sold as "cool and warm mist". The warm mode pre-heats the water before the piezo disc atomises it — it does not boil it
specs.whiteDust: Yes, in both modes. Warming the water does not change the mechanism: a piezo disc still aerosolises everything dissolved in it. the EPA's "Use and Care of Home Humidifiers" states that ultrasonic and impeller humidifiers "are very efficient at dispersing minerals in tap water into the air" and that they "can disperse materials, such as microorganisms and minerals, from their water tanks into indoor air". Dreo fits a mineral-absorption pad and sells no first-party replacement, so the aftermarket pads on Amazon are third-party and unverified
specs.outputPerDay: Published, unusually: 300 mL/hr in cool mist, 500 mL/hr in warm mist — 7.2 L/day and 12 L/day respectively if run continuously. Both exceed the 6 L tank, so the 60-hour runtime cannot be a high-output figure
specs.runtimeQuoted: "Up to 60 hours" — arithmetic settles this one. 6 L at the published 300 mL/hr cool-mist rate is 20 hours, and at 500 mL/hr warm it is 12. The 60-hour claim implies about 100 mL/hr, i.e. the lowest setting only
specs.coverage: Not published by Dreo on the product page — the only sizing language is the retail headline "for Large Room". Dreo publishes output instead, which is arguably the more useful number
specs.humidistat: Real closed-loop humidistat. Dreo rates the sensor at ±5% precision with a 30-90% RH adjustable target, plus manual, auto and sleep modes and 30 days of app-side history
specs.noiseLevel: 28 dB claimed by Dreo — a manufacturer figure with no independent measurement published, and comparable ultrasonics measure several dB higher in third-party testing
specs.consumables: A mineral-absorption pad sits in the tank. Dreo does not sell a first-party replacement pack; the only replacements listed are third-party multi-packs, so budget is unclear and the pad does not eliminate white dust regardless
specs.cleaningBurden: Top-fill opening takes a hand and the aroma tray lifts out, but the warm-mist heater adds a scale surface an ordinary cool-mist ultrasonic does not have. Nothing is dishwasher-safe. Dreo ships a cleaning guide and brush in the box, which is more than most
specs.antimicrobial: None claimed. No UV lamp, no antimicrobial coating. The warm mode is not hot enough to sterilise anything
specs.mistTemperature: This is the trap. Dreo's own spec says warm mode "reaches 86°F in 5 minutes" — 30°C, barely above body temperature. That is comfort, not sterilisation: a genuine warm-mist unit boils at 212°F. It also means the 280W warm mode buys you no hygiene benefit at all, and the mist is not sterile

pros: One of the very few humidifiers at any price that publishes a real output figure — 300 mL/hr cool, 500 mL/hr warm
Genuine closed-loop humidistat rated ±5% with a 30-90% setpoint range and 30 days of app history
6L top-fill tank plus app, Alexa and Google control for $89.99
Because output is published, you can actually compute the refill interval instead of trusting a runtime claim
cons: "Warm mist" tops out at 86°F by Dreo's own spec — warm water, not steam. It does not sterilise, and it costs 280W against 26W in cool mode
Ultrasonic in both modes, so it aerosolises minerals as white dust; the mineral-absorption pad reduces scale, it does not stop dust
The 60-hour runtime and the published 300-500 mL/hr output contradict each other — 6L at 300 mL/hr is 20 hours, so 60 hours is the lowest setting
Dreo sells no first-party replacement mineral pad; the only options are unverified third-party multi-packs
Twelve-month warranty and no published coverage figure or independent noise measurement
shortTagline: Warm mist that never boils: 86°F is comfort, not sterilisation.

model: Pure Enrichment MistAire Ultrasonic Cool Mist Humidifier (PEHUMIDIF)
material: Not published by the manufacturer; Pure Enrichment states the tank is BPA-free
connectivity: No wireless connectivity — two mist settings on a dial
features: Five-year warranty — the longest in this comparison by a factor of two
Published output: 120 mL/hr high, 60 mL/hr low
360° rotating mist nozzle and an optional night light
Automatic shut-off when the tank empties or is removed
12W draw — cheap enough to leave running all winter

specs.technology: Ultrasonic cool mist — a piezo disc atomises water into a visible plume
specs.whiteDust: Yes, and Pure Enrichment says so in its own catalogue: the MistAire Decalcification Cartridge Filter is described as reducing "white dust from minerals in tap water". It is a $12.99 accessory, not included, and Pure Enrichment recommends changing it every six months. the EPA's "Use and Care of Home Humidifiers" states that ultrasonic and impeller humidifiers "are very efficient at dispersing minerals in tap water into the air" and that they "can disperse materials, such as microorganisms and minerals, from their water tanks into indoor air"
specs.tankCapacity: 1.7 L / 0.45 gal — the smallest tank here after the Canopy
specs.outputPerDay: Published: 120 mL/hr on high and 60 mL/hr on low, i.e. 2.9 L/day and 1.4 L/day. That is a desk-scale output and Pure Enrichment is honest about it
specs.runtimeQuoted: Up to 25 hours on LOW, up to 12 hours on HIGH — Pure Enrichment publishes both, which almost nobody else in this set does
specs.coverage: Up to 250 ft² (Pure Enrichment) — the smallest claim here, and the only one that is consistent with the published output
specs.humidistat: None. Two mist settings on a dial and an auto shut-off for a dry tank. No humidity sensor, no auto mode, no readout
specs.noiseLevel: Not published as a decibel figure — Pure Enrichment says "whisper quiet". At 12W with no fan the noise is the ultrasonic hum and the water
specs.consumables: Optional decalcification cartridge at $12.99, changed every six months — about $26/yr if you use it. Nothing is required for the unit to run, but running it on tap water without the cartridge is what generates the dust
specs.cleaningBurden: Small, so it is quick, but the 1.7L tank neck is narrow and the supplied disk brush exists precisely because you cannot get a hand round the transducer. Nothing is dishwasher-safe. At 1.7L you are handling it daily anyway
specs.antimicrobial: None claimed. No UV, no antimicrobial coating, no bacteriostatic additive supported
specs.mistTemperature: Cool mist at room temperature — no burn risk, and no thermal kill step on the water

pros: A five-year warranty at $39.99, which no other humidifier in this comparison comes close to
Publishes both output (120/60 mL/hr) and runtimes for both settings — rare honesty at this price
Pure Enrichment openly sells a cartridge described as reducing "white dust from minerals in tap water", so the problem is at least acknowledged
12W and auto shut-off; small enough to sit on a desk without dominating it
cons: 1.7L and 120 mL/hr is a desk humidifier, not a bedroom one — a full tank on high lasts twelve hours and covers 250 ft² at best
Ultrasonic, so it makes white dust; the demineralisation cartridge that reduces it is a $12.99 accessory sold separately on a six-month cycle
No humidistat of any kind — two settings on a dial and nothing that senses the room
Narrow tank neck means you clean the transducer with the supplied brush rather than your hand
No antimicrobial or UV stage, and Pure Enrichment publishes no noise figure
shortTagline: $40, five-year warranty, 1.7 litres — a desk humidifier honest about its size.

model: Crane Drop EE-5301 Ultrasonic Cool Mist Humidifier
material: Plastic; retail listings describe a "Clean Control" antimicrobial additive in the tank material, which Crane's own manual does not mention
connectivity: No wireless connectivity — variable-output analogue knob
features: 1 gallon tank rated at 2.3 gallons of output per day
Variable-output knob rather than fixed steps
360° adjustable mist nozzle and a green/red water-level indicator
Detachable bottom-fill tank with a removable level sensor and cap
Optional Crane demineralisation filter for hard water

specs.technology: Ultrasonic cool mist — a piezo disc atomises water into a visible plume, no fan and no wick
specs.whiteDust: Yes, and Crane's own manual says so plainly: "filtered or distilled water is recommended to avoid white dust if tap water is too hard". Crane sells a demineralisation filter as an accessory, but retailers cannot agree on which one — Home Depot's listing cites HS-1932 and FiltersFast cites HS-3161. the EPA's "Use and Care of Home Humidifiers" states that ultrasonic and impeller humidifiers "are very efficient at dispersing minerals in tap water into the air" and that they "can disperse materials, such as microorganisms and minerals, from their water tanks into indoor air"
specs.outputPerDay: "Approx. 2.3 Gallon / 8.7 Liter" per Crane's manual — from a 1 gallon tank. Reaching rated output means filling it two and a bit times in 24 hours
specs.runtimeQuoted: Crane's manual gives both ends: "Max. up to 24 hours / Min. 11 Hours". Retail listings quote only the 24-hour figure, which is the lowest output setting
specs.coverage: Sources conflict outright: Crane's own manual says "Up to 250 sq. ft. / 23 m2", while Home Depot and Lowe's list the identical EE-5301 at up to 500 ft² — a 2x discrepancy between the manufacturer's manual and its own retail listings
specs.humidistat: None. A variable-output knob and an auto shut-off for a dry tank. There is no humidity sensor and no auto mode anywhere in the Drop line
specs.noiseLevel: Not published as a decibel figure — the manual and retail listings say only "whisper quiet". No fan, so the noise is the ultrasonic hum
specs.consumables: Nothing required — Crane's design is explicitly filter-optional. The demineralisation filter is an accessory whose part number varies by retailer; distilled water is the alternative, at roughly $1-1.50/gal
specs.cleaningBurden: Crane's manual asks for daily emptying and a weekly deep clean: half a gallon of warm water plus two tablespoons of white vinegar in the tank, shaken and left 20-30 minutes, then repeated for the basin. The tank has a detachable bottom cap and a removable level sensor, which genuinely helps. Nothing is dishwasher-safe
specs.antimicrobial: Claimed by retailers, absent from the manual. Home Depot's listing says the unit is "made with clean control anti-microbial material which reduces mold and bacteria growth by up to 99.96%"; FiltersFast's listing for the same model says no antimicrobial claims are made, and Crane's own manual contains no such claim. Treat the 99.96% figure as unsubstantiated
specs.mistTemperature: Cool mist at room temperature — no burn risk, no heater, no thermal kill step

pros: Crane's manual is unusually honest — it publishes 2.3 gal/day output, both ends of the runtime range, and tells you outright to use filtered or distilled water to avoid white dust
Detachable bottom cap and removable water-level sensor make the tank genuinely easier to clean than most ultrasonics
Variable-output knob rather than two or three fixed steps, so you can dial in a low continuous rate
A gallon of capacity and six colour options for $44.99
cons: Crane's own manual (250 ft²) and its own retail listings (500 ft²) disagree by a factor of two on coverage, and by nearly $21 on price
Ultrasonic white dust, and the demineralisation accessory has two different part numbers depending on which retailer you ask (HS-1932 vs HS-3161)

The "reduces mold and bacteria growth by up to 99.96%" antimicrobial claim appears on retail listings and nowhere in Crane's manual — another retailer says the model makes no antimicrobial claims at all
2.3 gal/day rated output from a 1 gallon tank means two-plus refills a day to hit the number
No humidistat, no humidity readout, and a one-year warranty against five on the cheaper Pure Enrichment
shortTagline: A nursery classic whose own manual and its retail listings disagree on almost everything.
